cards.heading: Nipkow disk
cards.text: A Nipkow disk (sometimes Anglicized as Nipkov disk; patented in 1884), also known as scanning disk, is a mechanical, rotating, geometrically operating image scanning device, patented by Paul Gottlieb Nipkow in Berlin. This scanning disk was a fundamental component in mechanical television, and thus the first televisions, through the 1920s and 1930s.

main.title: Benz Patent-Motorwagen
main.summary: The Benz Patent-Motorwagen ("patent motorcar") was the world's first practical production automobile, built by Benz & Cie between 1885 and 1893.

cards.heading: Benz Patent-Motorwagen
cards.text:
The Benz Patent-Motorwagen ("patent motorcar") was the world's first practical production automobile, built by Benz & Cie between 1885 and 1893. Featuring three wheels, a single-cylinder four-stroke engine and belt-drive, Benz & Cie used the designation "Patent-Motorwagen" for their four-wheel cars until c.1900, but these are known today by their other names, such as Viktoria and Velo. All these cars used the same layout and belt-drive technology for which Benz received patent number DRP37435 in 1886, hence the designation.

The original Patent-Motorwagen was developed over the period 1884 – 1887 by the German engineer Carl Benz and is widely regarded as the first practical automobile.

The engine's output was stabilised by a flywheel. In the first vehicles this was horizontal and the vehicles had a single belt-drive. Later vehicles had a vertical flywheel and two belt-drives. Each belt-drive gave a single transmission ratio; from 1886 the single-belt-drive vehicles also had a reduction gearbox which provided a second transmission ratio.

main.title: Statue of Liberty
main.summary: Dedicated on October 28, 1886, the Statue of Liberty was a gift from France to the United States.

cards.heading: Statue of Liberty
cards.text:
The Statue of Liberty (Liberty Enlightening the World, French: La Liberté éclairant le monde; colloquially known as Lady Liberty) is a colossal neoclassical sculpture of a robed and crowned woman on Liberty Island, part of New York City, in New York Harbor. The copper-clad statue, a gift to the United States from the people of France, was designed by French sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, and its metal framework built by Gustave Eiffel. The statue was dedicated on October 28, 1886.

The statue is a figure of a classically draped woman, inspired by the Roman goddess of liberty, Libertas. She holds a torch above her head with her right hand, and in her left hand carries a tabula ansata inscribed JULY IV MDCCLXXVI (July 4, 1776, in Roman numerals), the date of the U.S. Declaration of Independence. With her left foot she steps on a broken chain and shackle, commemorating the national abolition of slavery following the American Civil War.

main.title: Michelson–Morley experiment
main.summary: Albert Michelson and Edward Morley carried out their experiment in Cleveland between April and July 1887, publishing the results that November.

cards.heading: Michelson–Morley experiment
cards.text: Albert Michelson and Edward Morley carried out their experiment in Cleveland between April and July 1887, publishing the results that November. They compared light travelling in perpendicular directions, looking for the effect of Earth's motion through the supposed luminiferous aether. They found no significant difference. The result challenged theories that treated aether as the medium carrying light waves and prompted further investigation into light and motion. That research formed part of the scientific path towards special relativity, which would describe these relationships without motion relative to an aether.

main.title: Tesla's alternating-current motor patents
main.summary: Nikola Tesla received patents for his alternating-current motor system in May 1888 and presented his work that month. Galileo Ferraris was also developing motors based on a rotating magnetic field.

cards.heading: Tesla's alternating-current motor patents
cards.text:
Nikola Tesla received patents for his alternating-current motor system in May 1888 and presented his work that month. Galileo Ferraris was also developing motors based on a rotating magnetic field.

An AC motor is an electric motor driven by an alternating current (AC). The AC motor commonly consists of two basic parts, an outside stator having coils supplied with alternating current to produce a rotating magnetic field, and an inside rotor attached to the output shaft producing a second rotating magnetic field. The rotor magnetic field may be produced by permanent magnets, reluctance saliency, or DC or AC electrical windings.

Less common, AC linear motors operate on similar principles as rotating motors but have their stationary and moving parts arranged in a straight line configuration, producing linear motion instead of rotation.

main.title: The Kodak camera arrives
main.summary: The Kodak camera appeared in 1888, bringing photography with roll film to a wider public.

cards.heading: The Kodak camera arrives
cards.text: The Kodak camera appeared in 1888, bringing photography with roll film to a wider public. George Eastman and Henry A. Strong had formed their partnership to develop such a camera; Eastman Kodak was incorporated in 1892. Film became the centre of a business that grew into one of the world's largest photographic manufacturers. Later models such as the Brownie and Instamatic continued its mass-market approach. The 1888 camera marks the beginning of that connection between a simple consumer product and the film industry supporting it.

main.title: Eiffel Tower
main.summary: The Eiffel Tower is a wrought-iron lattice tower built in Paris as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair.

cards.heading: Eiffel Tower
cards.text:
The Eiffel Tower (French: Tour Eiffel) is a lattice tower on the Champ de Mars in Paris, France. It is named after the engineer Gustave Eiffel, whose company designed and built the tower from 1887 to 1889.

Locally nicknamed "La dame de fer" (French for "Iron Lady") for its use of wrought iron, it was constructed as the centrepiece of the 1889 World's Fair, and to crown the centennial anniversary of the French Revolution. Although initially criticised by some of France's leading artists and intellectuals for its design, it has since become a global cultural icon of France and one of the most recognisable structures in the world. The tower received 5,889,000 visitors in 2022. The Eiffel Tower is the most visited monument with an entrance fee in the world: 6.91 million people ascended it in 2015. It was designated a monument historique in 1964, and was named part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site ("Paris, Banks of the Seine") in 1991.

main.title: Charlie Chaplin
main.subtitle: Born in London: a performer who made movement tell a story
main.summary: Charles Spencer Chaplin was born in London on 16 April 1889. His childhood brought hardship and early experience of performing, before stage work carried him toward cinema. As actor, director, writer and composer, he developed an unusually close control over his films. The Tramp's clothes and movements gave audiences a figure they could recognise before he had explained anything about himself.

cards.heading: Born into a performing family
cards.text: Charles Spencer Chaplin was born in London on 16 April 1889. His childhood brought hardship and early experience of performing, before stage work carried him toward cinema. As actor, director, writer and composer, he developed an unusually close control over his films. The Tramp's clothes and movements gave audiences a figure they could recognise before he had explained anything about himself.

cards.heading: The invention of the Tramp
cards.text: Chaplin's early training included dance and comedy, and his American tours with Fred Karno led to work in motion pictures. The Tramp emerged in 1914: the small hat, cane, tight coat and oversized shoes created a body full of mismatched proportions. The character could appear dignified while desperately improvising. A meal, a doorway or a machine became the basis of an encounter, with a precisely timed physical action carrying embarrassment, defiance or affection.

cards.heading: Comedy with an emotional history
cards.text: The Kid, City Lights and Modern Times joined sustained comic invention to relationships shaped by poverty, work and vulnerability. Chaplin continued to use gesture and music as sound cinema developed, then turned to speech in The Great Dictator's final address. In 1972 he returned to the United States to receive an honorary Academy Award. His brief, emotional response followed an extended ovation, making the ceremony another public encounter between the performer and audiences who had grown up with his films.

main.title: Herman Hollerith: punched cards for the census
main.summary: The 1890 United States census used Herman Hollerith’s punched-card tabulating system to process its data.

cards.heading: Herman Hollerith: punched cards for the census
cards.text:
The 1890 United States census used Herman Hollerith’s punched-card tabulating system to process its data.

Herman Hollerith (February 29, 1860 – November 17, 1929) was a German-American statistician, inventor, and businessman who developed an electromechanical tabulating machine for punched cards to assist in summarizing information and, later, in accounting. His invention of the punched card tabulating machine, patented in 1884, marks the beginning of the era of mechanized binary code and semiautomatic data processing systems, and his concept dominated that landscape for nearly a century.

Hollerith founded a company that was amalgamated in 1911 with several other companies to form the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company. In 1924, the company was renamed "International Business Machines" (IBM) and became one of the largest and most successful companies of the 20th century. Hollerith is regarded as one of the seminal figures in the development of data processing.

main.title: Naismith invents basketball
main.subtitle: An indoor game for a New England winter
main.summary: James Naismith devised basketball in Springfield in December 1891; its first game is commemorated on 21 December.

cards.heading: An indoor game for a New England winter
cards.text: James Naismith devised basketball in December 1891 at the International YMCA Training School in Massachusetts, now Springfield College. His supervisor, Luther Gulick, wanted an engaging indoor activity for winter. Naismith used a football, two peach baskets mounted above the floor and thirteen rules. The first players formed teams of nine, and passing was essential because running with the ball was forbidden. The first game is commemorated on December 21; the rules appeared in the school magazine in January 1892. Students carried the sport elsewhere, while later changes introduced dribbling and open-bottomed nets.

sources.title: James Naismith and the invention of basketball
